technical-data.invention-title: BEVERAGE PRODUCTS HAVING SUPERIOR VITAMIN STABILITY
PRODUITS POUR BOISSONS A STABLITE VITAMINIQUE SUPERIEURE

abstract.p: Disclosed are beverage products with improved vitamin stability. The beverage products include an effective amount of a aminpolycarboxylic acid as well as an effective amount of a polyphosphate, and can be enriched with one or more vitamins or other nutrients. In one embodiment, the beverage products include added water, fruit juice, ascorbic acid, ethylene tetra-acetic acid (EDTA), sodium hexametaphosphate, and potassium sorbate. The beverage can be packaged in relatively inexpensive HDPE-type containers which are generally oxygen permeable, and do not require the use of special oxygen barrier packaging to preserve the vitamins and flavor oils from oxidation.

L'invention concerne des produits pour boissons à stabilité vitaminique supérieure, comprenant une dose efficace d'acide aminopolycarboxylique, de même qu'une dose efficace d'un polyphosphate, et que l'on peut enrichir à l'aide d'une ou plusieurs vitamines ou d'autres nutriments. Dans un mode de réalisation, on a ajouté à ces produits de l'eau, des jus de fruits, de l'acide ascorbique, de l'acide d'éthylènediamine tétracétique, de l'hexamétaphosphate de sodium et du sorbate de potassium. On peut conditionner ces boissons dans des contenants du type polyéthylène haute densité, relativement bons marché, généralement perméables à l'oxygène et ne nécessitant pas l'utilisation d'un emballage spécial comprenant une barrière à oxygène pour empêcher l'oxydation des vitamines et des huiles aromatisées.

description.p: BEVERAGE PRODUCTS HAVING SUPERIOR VITAMIN STABILITY
FIELD OF THE INVENTION
The present invention relates to beverage products, such as carbonated and noncarbonated beverage products containing fruit juice and having supenor vitamin and flavor stability
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Controlling vitamin and flavor stability of dilute juice beverages is an ongoing concern among beverage manufacturers It is important that beverages maintain their intended flavor charactenstics and nutπtional charactenstics, even after prolonged penods of shelf storage

One source of flavor degradation is microbial growth Another source of flavor degradation is oxidation of certam unsaturated compounds Additionally, oxidation can also be a cause of degradation of vitamin compounds For instance, certain water soluble vitamins, oil soluble vitamins, flavor oils, and flavor essences can be degraded by oxidation if dissolved oxygen is present in the beverage container Microbial degradation can result from accidental inoculation of the beverage products during manufacturing or packagmg Food spoilage microorganisms can then rapidly proliferate by feeding on nutnents provided by the fruit juice component of the noncarbonated dilute juice beverages Flavor degradation and vitamin degradation due to oxidation can occur when dissolved oxygen and a catalyst, such as metal ions, are present m the packaged beverage, or when the beverage package is relatively oxygen permeable, such as m the case of relatively mexpensive plastic packagmg, such as high density polyethylene (HDPE) packages Such plastic containers can provide a relatively poor barner to oxygen, when compared to containers made of glass or metal Oxygen passmg through the container can cause oxidation of beverage ingredients which include water and oil soluble components, mcludmg vitamins and flavor components including flavor oils This oxidation can result m the loss of vitamin content and the formation of undesirable flavors and/or odors

Microbial stability in dilute beverage products can be provided to some extent by heat pasteurizing during packagmg (hot packing) or by packagmg under completely aseptic conditions (aseptic packagmg) Special packagmg constructions for providing a barner between oxygen m the atmosphere and the beverage can also be used to reduce the amount of oxygen that enters the beverage over time However, such processing or packagmg methods are generally undesirable from a cost and complexity standpomt Also, flexible containers made from polymenc matenals, such as high density polyethylene, which have
become more popular with consumers, should not be subjected to the pasteurization temperatures utilized during hot packing operations

U S Patent 5,431,940 to Calderas et al discloses a beverage contammg a polyphosphate and a preservative for beverage products that are to be stored at ambient temperatures for at least about 10 days without substantial microbial proliferation One disadvantage associated with the polyphosphate disclosed m TJ S Patent 5,431,940 is that, over tune, the effectiveness of the polyphosphate as a chelatmg agent may be reduced Without bemg limited by theory, it is believed that the cham length of the polyphosphate can be reduced over time, such as by hydrolysis
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

Accordingly, Applicants have found that it would be desirable to provide a beverage product which has the antimicrobial effectiveness of a polyphosphate and preservative combination, yet maintains chelation activity m the beverage for a substantially longer penod of time than is provided by polyphosphates

Applicants have discovered that dilute juice beverages fortified with vitamins can lose at least some vitamin content to oxidation, despite the use of a polyphosphate and preservative combination Without bemg limited by theory, it is believed that trace metal ions in the beverage can be a food source for microbes, and can also serve as a catalyst for oxidation of compounds such as vitamins and flavor oils Accordmg to one embodiment of the present mvention, a beverage composition is provided having a first chelatmg agent, which can compnse an aminopolycarboxylic acid, such as ethylene diamine tetra-acetic acid (EDTA), and a second chelatmg agent, which can comprise a polyphosphate The first chelatmg agent provides chelatmg properties over an extended length of time as compared to the second chelatmg agent, and is present in quantities effective to reduce the rate of oxidation of vitamins and flavor oils The second chelatmg agent provides chelatmg properties over a relatively shorter penod of time as compared to the first chelatmg agent The second chelatmg agent can have a rate of degradation by hydrolysis which is greater than that of the first chelatmg agent

The second chelatmg agent, m combination with a preservative, is present m quantities effective to kill microbes which may be present durmg the initial packagmg of the beverage The presence of second chelatmg agent is effective m reducmg microbial activity durmg the early portion of the beverage's shelf life, while the first chelatmg agent provides sustamed chelatmg activity to preserve vitamins and flavor compounds in the beverage over longer periods of time

TEST METHODS
Test Method: Microbial Stability

The term "microbial proliferation" as used herein means a 100 fold increase or greater in the number of beverage spoilage microorganisms in a noncarbonated beverage product after an initial inoculation level of about 10 cfu/ml. Beverage products described as "microbially stable" exhibit less than a 100 fold increase in the level of microorganisms when stored at 73°F for at least 28 days, following an initial contamination level of 10 cfu/ml of spoilage microorganisms. Beverages described as "microbially unstable" exhibit more than a 100 fold increase in the level of microorganisms when stored at 73°F for 28 days, following an initial contamination level of 10 cfu/ml of spoilage microorganisms. The microbial stability a noncarbonated beverage product can be determined by the following method. Beverage products are inoculated with mixed groups of preservative resistant yeast containing at least four separate yeast isolates, including Zygosaccharomyces bailii, and with mixed groups of preservative resistant, acid tolerant bacteria, including Acetobacter species. All yeast and bacteria utilized in the inoculation are previously isolated from preserved fruit juice beverages. Inoculated beverage products are maintained at 20°C for at least 60 days and aerobic plate cultures performed periodically. Aerobic plate counts of both yeast and bacteria populations are performed as described in the Compendium of Methods for the Microbiological Examinations of Foods, American Public Health Association, Washington, D.C. (edited by C. Vanderzant and D.F. Splittstoesser), which description is incorporated herein by reference. These plate counts are then used to identify the degree of microbial proliferation in the inoculated beverage product.
